Key Research Thinking Patterns: Cross-Modality Data Fusion: Combining data from different sensors or sources to overcome the limitations of a single source. (e.g., Using higher axial resolution PET data to find intervertebral boundaries that are poorly defined in low-dose CT scans; jointly considering MWIR and LWIR detections to improve recall for small objects compared to either band alone).

Multi-Level Validation: Validating a computational method across simulated, controlled laboratory, and complex real-world data. (e.g., Testing analytic-signal backbone extraction first on simulated harmonic oscillators, then on data from a physical lab-scale SDOF model, before analyzing complex signals).

Foundational Problem Isolation: Analyzing a fundamental, linear, or simplified component of a complex system to understand its core principles before tackling nonlinearity. (e.g., Focusing on the linear unforced harmonic oscillator to pinpoint theoretical and computational issues in backbone extraction, which is a prerequisite for analyzing nonlinear systems).

Bottleneck-Driven Innovation: Creating novel algorithms or transforms to solve a clearly-defined weakness in existing computational pipelines. (e.g., Developing a new real, integer-valued 8x8 Hirschman transform specifically to improve quantization performance relative to the standard DCT; applying the Mirror Periodic Method (MPM) to specifically reduce "end effects" in Hilbert transform computations).
Summary Description: Dr. Joseph P. Havlicek specializes in Digital Signal and Image Processing, focusing on cross-disciplinary applications in medical imaging, video coding, and sensor system analysis. His research involves developing and applying advanced computational methods, including novel (Hirschman) and established (Hilbert) transforms, deep learning models (U-Nets, YOLOv4) , and multi-modal data fusion (PET-CT, DBIR). Key applications of his work include automating quantitative analysis in PET/CT scans for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) patients, creating new transforms for efficient video compression, enhancing small object detection in dual-band infrared video, and identifying parameters in dynamic systems for applications like earthquake engineering.
